claim: PI3Kβ is functionally unique in the ability to integrate signals derived from receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), G-protein coupled receptors, and Rho-family GTPases.
source: Phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) beta (PI3Kβ) is functionally unique in the ability to integrate signals derived from receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), G-protein coupled receptors, and Rho-family GTPases.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of PI3Kβ.

claim: Auto-inhibited PI3Kβ prioritizes interactions with RTK-derived tyrosine phosphorylated (pY) peptides before engaging either GβGγ or Rac1(GTP).
source: We find that auto-inhibited PI3Kβ prioritizes interactions with RTK-derived tyrosine phosphorylated (pY) peptides before engaging either GβGγ or Rac1(GTP).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: pY peptides strongly localize PI3Kβ to membranes, but stimulation of lipid kinase activity is modest.
source: Although pY peptides strongly localize PI3Kβ to membranes, stimulation of lipid kinase activity is modest.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 1 and 5.

claim: PI3Kβ activity is dramatically enhanced beyond what can be explained by simply increasing membrane localization in the presence of either pY/GβGγ or pY/Rac1(GTP).
source: In the presence of either pY/GβGγ or pY/Rac1(GTP), PI3Kβ activity is dramatically enhanced beyond what can be explained by simply increasing membrane localization.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by kinetic data in Figure 5.

claim: PI3Kβ is synergistically activated by pY/GβGγ and pY/Rac1(GTP) through a mechanism consistent with allosteric regulation.
source: Instead, PI3Kβ is synergistically activated by pY/GβGγ and pY/Rac1 (GTP) through a mechanism consistent with allosteric regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by the kinetic analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Class I PI3Ks catalyze the phosphorylation of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P2] to generate PI(3,4,5)P3.
source: Serving a critical role in cell signaling, the class I family of PI3Ks catalyze the phosphorylation of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate [PI(4,5)P2] to generate PI(3,4,5)P3.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PI3K function stated in the introduction.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 is a low-abundance lipid (<0.05%) in the plasma membrane.
source: Although a low-abundance lipid (<0.05%) in the plasma membrane (Wenk et al., 2003; Nasuhoglu et al., 2002; Stephens et al., 1993), PI(3,4,5)P3 can increase 40-fold following receptor activation (Stephens et al., 1991; Parent et al., 1998; Insall and Weiner, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 can increase 40-fold following receptor activation.
source: Although a low-abundance lipid (<0.05%) in the plasma membrane (Wenk et al., 2003; Nasuhoglu et al., 2002; Stephens et al., 1993), PI(3,4,5)P3 can increase 40-fold following receptor activation (Stephens et al., 1991; Parent et al., 1998; Insall and Weiner, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Misregulation of the PI3K signaling pathway can result in constitutively high levels of PI(3,4,5)P3 that are detrimental to cell health.
source: Although signal adaptation mechanisms typically restore PI(3,4,5)P3 to the basal level following receptor activation (Funamoto et al., 2002; Yip et al., 2008; Auger et al., 1989), misregulation of the PI3K signaling pathway can result in constitutively high levels of PI(3,4,5)P3 that are detrimental to cell health.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids serve an instructive role in driving actin-based membrane protrusions.
source: Since PI(3,4,5)P3lipids serve an instructive role in driving actin-based membrane protrusions (Howard and Oresajo, 1985; Weiner, 2002; Graziano et al., 2017), sustained PI(3,4,5)P3 signaling is known to drive cancer cell metastasis (Hanker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sustained PI(3,4,5)P3 signaling is known to drive cancer cell metastasis.
source: Since PI(3,4,5)P3lipids serve an instructive role in driving actin-based membrane protrusions (Howard and Oresajo, 1985; Weiner, 2002; Graziano et al., 2017), sustained PI(3,4,5)P3 signaling is known to drive cancer cell metastasis (Hanker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hanker et al., 2013.

claim: Elevated PI(3,4,5)P3 levels stimulate the AKT signaling pathway and Tec family kinases, which can drive cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis.
source: Elevated PI(3,4,5)P3 levels also stimulates the AKT signaling pathway and Tec family kinases, which can drive cellular proliferation and tumorigenesis (Manning and Cantley, 2007; Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Manning and Cantley, 2007 and Fruman et al., 2017.

claim: Class IA PI3Ks are thought to reside in the cytoplasm as auto-inhibited heterodimeric protein complexes in the absence of a stimulatory input.
source: In the absence of a stimulatory input, the class IA family of PI3Ks (PI3Kα, PI3Kβ, PI3Kδ) are thought to reside in the cytoplasm as auto-inhibited heterodimeric protein complexes composed of a catalytic (p110α, p110β, or p110δ) and regulatory subunit (p85α, p85β, p55γ, p50α, or p55α) (Burke, 2018; Vadas et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burke, 2018 and Vadas et al., 2011.

claim: The inter-SH2 (iSH2) domain of the regulatory subunit tightly associates with the ABD of the catalytic subunit, providing structural integrity while limiting dynamic conformational changes.
source: The inter-SH2 (iSH2) domain of the regulatory subunit tightly associates with the ABD of the catalytic subunit (Yu et al., 1998), providing structural integrity, while limiting dynamic conformational changes.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 1998.

claim: The nSH2 and cSH2 domains of the regulatory subunit form additional inhibitory contacts that limit the conformational dynamics of the catalytic subunit.
source: The nSH2 and cSH2 domains of the regulatory subunit form additional inhibitory contacts that limit the conformational dynamics of the catalytic subunit (Zhang et al., 2011; Mandelker et al., 2009; Burke et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 1993; Yu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: PI3Kβ is uniquely capable of interacting with Rho-family GTPases, Rab GTPases, heterotrimeric G-protein complexes (GβGγ), and phosphorylated receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs).
source: Among the class IA PI3Ks, PI3Kβ is uniquely capable of interacting with Rho-family GTPases (Fritsch et al., 2013), Rab GTPases (Christoforidis et al., 1999; Heitz et al., 2019), heterotrimeric G-protein complexes (GβGγ) (Kurosu et al., 1997; Maier et al., 1999; Guillermet-Guibert et al., 2008), and phosphorylated receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) (Zhang et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Interactions with RTK derived phosphotyrosine peptides release nSH2 and cSH2-mediated inhibition of the catalytic subunit to stimulate PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity.
source: Like other class IA PI3Ks, interactions with RTK derived phosphotyrosine peptides release nSH2 and cSH2-mediated inhibition of the catalytic subunit to stimulate PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity (Dbouk et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dbouk et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: GβGγ and Rac1(GTP) in solution have been shown to stimulate PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity.
source: GβGγ and Rac1(GTP) in solution have also been shown to stimulate PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity (Dbouk et al., 2012; Fritsch et al., 2013; Maier et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of Rho-family GTPases stimulates PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity in cells.
source: Similarly, activation of Rho-family GTPases (Fritsch et al., 2013) and G-protein coupled receptors (Houslay et al., 2016) in cells, stimulates PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fritsch et al., 2013 and Houslay et al., 2016.

claim: Studies in neutrophils and in vitro biochemistry suggest that PI3Kβ is synergistically activated through coincidence detection of RTKs and GβGγ.
source: Studies in neutrophils and in vitro biochemistry suggest that PI3Kβ is synergistically activated through coincidence detection of RTKs and GβGγ (Houslay et al., 2016; Dbouk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Houslay et al., 2016 and Dbouk et al., 2012.

claim: Rac1(GTP) and GβGγ have been reported to synergistically activate PI3Kβ in cells.
source: Similarly, Rac1(GTP) and GβGγ have been reported to synergistically activate PI3Kβ in cells (Erami et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Erami et al., 2017.

claim: An enhanced membrane recruitment mechanism is the most prominent model used to explain synergistic activation of PI3Ks.
source: An enhanced membrane recruitment mechanism is the most prominent model used to explain synergistic activation of PI3Ks.
evidence: This is stated as the prevailing model in the field.

claim: Previous biochemical studies of PI3Kβ have utilized solution-based assays to measure P(3,4,5)P3 production.
source: There is limited kinetic data examining how PI3Kβ is regulated by different membrane-tethered proteins. Previous biochemical studies of PI3Kβ have utilized solution-based assays to measure P(3,4,5)P3 production.
evidence: This describes the limitations of previous experimental approaches.

claim: Previous studies concerning the synergistic activation of PI3Ks are challenging to interpret because RTK-derived peptides are always presented in solution alongside membrane-anchored signaling inputs.
source: Previous studies concerning the synergistic activation of PI3Ks are challenging to interpret because RTK-derived peptides are always presented in solution alongside membrane-anchored signaling inputs.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous experimental approaches.

claim: All the common signaling inputs for PI3K activation (i.e. RTKs, GβGγ, Rac1/Cdc42) are membrane-associated proteins.
source: However, all the common signaling inputs for PI3K activation (i.e. RTKs, GβGγ, Rac1/Cdc42) are membrane-associated proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about PI3K signaling inputs.

claim: Activation of class 1A PI3Ks has never been reconstituted using solely membrane-tethered activators conjugated to membranes in a biologically relevant configuration.
source: Activation of class 1A PI3Ks has never been reconstituted using solely membrane-tethered activators conjugated to membranes in a biologically relevant configuration.
evidence: This describes a gap in the field that this study addresses.

claim: Membrane docking of PI3Kβ first requires interactions with RTK-derived tyrosine phosphorylated (pY) peptides, while PI3Kβ localization is insensitive to membranes that contain either Rac1(GTP) or GβGγ alone.
source: Overall, we found that membrane docking of PI3Kβ first requires interactions with RTK-derived tyrosine phosphorylated (pY) peptides, while PI3Kβ localization is insensitive to membranes that contain either Rac1(GTP) or GβGγ alone.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Following engagement with a pY peptide, PI3Kβ can associate with either GβGγ or Rac1(GTP).
source: Following engagement with a pY peptide, PI3Kβ can associate with either GβGγ or Rac1(GTP).
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results section and supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: For synergistic PI3Kβ localization mediated by pY/GβGγ, it's essential for the nSH2 domain to move away from the GβGγ binding site.
source: In the case of synergistic PI3Kβ localization mediated by pY/GβGγ, it's essential for the nSH2 domain to move away from the GβGγ binding site.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3 and AlphaFold modeling.

claim: The PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) and PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complexes display a ~2-fold increase in membrane localization.
source: Although both the PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) and PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complexes display a ~2-fold increase in membrane localization, the corresponding increase in catalytic efficiency is much greater.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the results section and supported by data in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: The increase in catalytic efficiency for PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) and PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complexes is much greater than the increase in membrane localization.
source: Although both the PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) and PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complexes display a ~2-fold increase in membrane localization, the corresponding increase in catalytic efficiency is much greater.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Synergistic activation of PI3Kβ depends on allosteric modulation of lipid kinase activity.
source: Overall, our results indicate that synergistic activation of PI3Kβ depends on allosteric modulation of lipid kinase activity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the results section and supported by kinetic data in Figure 5.

claim: Only the tyrosine phosphorylated peptide (pY) could robustly localize Dy647-PI3Kβ to supported membranes when comparing pY, Rac1(GTP), or GβGγ.
source: Comparing membrane localization of Dy647-PI3Kβ in the presence of pY, Rac1(GTP), or GβGγ revealed that only the tyrosine phosphorylated peptide (pY) could robustly localize Dy647-PI3Kβ to supported membranes (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Prioritization of pY interactions was consistently observed across a variety of membrane lipid compositions.
source: This prioritization of interactions was consistently observed across a variety of membrane lipid compositions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing the anionic lipid charge of supported membranes through the addition of 20% phosphatidylserine (PS) did not significantly change the frequency of Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane interactions in the presence of either Rac1(GTP) or GβGγ alone.
source: Increasing the anionic lipid charge of supported membranes through the addition of 20% phosphatidylserine (PS), did not significantly change the frequency of Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane interactions in the presence of either Rac1(GTP) or GβGγ alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The binding frequency of Dy647-PI3Kβ to membranes with GβGγ alone was reduced 2000-fold compared to measurements on pY membranes.
source: Although we could detect some transient Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane binding events in the presence of GβGγ alone, the binding frequency was reduced 2000-fold compared to our measurements on pY membranes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Localization of wild-type Dy647-PI3Kβ phenocopied the GβGγ binding mutant, Dy647-PI3Kβ (K532D, K533D), indicating that low-frequency binding events are mostly mediated by lipid interactions rather than direct binding to GβGγ.
source: Localization of wild-type Dy647-PI3Kβ phenocopied the GβGγ binding mutant, Dy647-PI3Kβ (K532D, K533D), indicating that the low-frequency binding events we observed are mostly mediated by lipid interactions rather than direct binding to GβGγ (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 comparing wild-type and mutant PI3Kβ.

claim: The addition of 20% PS lipids caused a subtle increase in the number of Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane binding observed when 20 µM pY peptide was added in solution.
source: The addition of 20% PS lipids did, however, cause a subtle increase in the number of Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane binding observed when 20 µM pY peptide was added in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dy647-PI3Kβ can cooperatively bind to one doubly phosphorylated peptide derived from the PDGF receptor.
source: Based on our single molecule dwell time and diffusion analysis, Dy647-PI3Kβ can cooperatively bind to one doubly phosphorylated peptide derived from the PDGF receptor.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on single molecule analysis shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Dy647-PI3Kβ with a mutated nSH2 or cSH2 domain that eliminates pY binding still displayed membrane diffusivity indistinguishable from wild-type PI3Kβ.
source: Supporting this model, Dy647-PI3Kβ with a mutated nSH2 or cSH2 domain that eliminates pY binding, still displayed membrane diffusivity indistinguishable from wild-type PI3Kβ.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2J and Table 1.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of membrane-bound pY-PI3Kβ complexes did not significantly change over a broad range of pY membrane surface densities that span three orders of magnitude.
source: The diffusion coefficient of membrane-bound pY-PI3Kβ complexes also did not significantly change over a broad range of pY membrane surface densities that span three orders of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: The nSH2(R358A) and cSH2(R649A) mutants showed a 60% and 75% reduction in membrane localization at equilibrium, respectively, compared to wild-type Dy647-PI3Kβ.
source: Compared to wild-type Dy647-PI3Kβ, the nSH2(R358A) and cSH2(R649A) mutants showed a 60% and 75% reduction in membrane localization at equilibrium, respectively (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Single molecule dwell time analysis showed a significant reduction in membrane affinity for Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2(R358A) and cSH2(R649A) compared to wild-type PI3Kβ.
source: Single molecule dwell time analysis also showed a significant reduction in membrane affinity for Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2(R358A) and cSH2(R649A) compared to wild-type PI3Kβ (Figure 2I and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2I and Table 1.

claim: Single molecule diffusion of membrane-bound nSH2(R358A) and cSH2(R649A) mutants were nearly identical to wild-type Dy647-PI3Kβ.
source: Single molecule diffusion (or mobility) of membrane-bound nSH2(R358A) and cSH2(R649A) mutants, however, were nearly identical to wild-type Dy647-PI3Kβ (Figure 2J and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2J and Table 1.

claim: A two-fold increase in membrane localization was observed due to synergistic association with pY and GβGγ.
source: Comparing the bulk membrane absorption of Dy647-PI3Kβ in the presence of pY alone, we observed a two-fold increase in membrane localization due to synergistic association with pY and GβGγ (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Single molecule imaging experiments showed a 1.9-fold increase in the membrane dwell time of Dy647-PI3Kβ in the presence of both pY and GβGγ.
source: Single molecule imaging experiments also showed a 1.9-fold increase in the membrane dwell time of Dy647-PI3Kβ in the presence of both pY and GβGγ (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A 22% reduction in the average single-particle displacement and a decrease in the diffusion coefficient was observed due to ternary complex formation with pY and GβGγ.
source: Consistent with Dy647-PI3Kβ forming a complex with pY and GβGγ, we observed a 22% reduction in the average single-particle displacement and a decrease in the diffusion coefficient due to ternary complex formation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The p85α(nSH2) domain is predicted to sterically block GβGγ binding to p110β based on AlphaFold Multimer modeling.
source: Using AlphaFold Multimer (Evans et al., 2022; Jumper et al., 2021), we created a model that illustrates how the p85α(nSH2) domain is predicted to sterically block GβGγ binding to p110β.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold Multimer modeling shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2(R358A) mutant tethered to membrane-conjugated pY peptide was unable to engage membrane-anchored GβGγ.
source: Further supporting this model, we found that the Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2(R358A) mutant tethered to membrane-conjugated pY peptide was unable to engage membrane-anchored GβGγ.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A 1.4-fold enhancement in Dy647-PI3Kβ localization was observed due to active Rac1 on membranes containing either pY-Rac1(GDP) or pY-Rac1(GTP).
source: Bulk localization to membranes containing either pY-Rac1(GDP) or pY-Rac1(GTP), revealed that active Rac1 could enhance Dy647-PI3Kβ localization 1.4-fold (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Single molecule analysis revealed a 1.5-fold increase in the mean dwell time of Dy647-PI3Kβ in the presence of pY-Rac1(GTP).
source: Similarly, single molecule analysis revealed a 1.5-fold increase in the mean dwell time of Dy647-PI3Kβ in the presence of pY-Rac1(GTP) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The average displacement of Dy647-PI3Kβ per frame decreased by 28% in the presence of pY and Rac1(GTP).
source: The average displacement of Dy647-PI3Kβ per frame (i.e. 52 ms) also decreased by 28% in the presence of pY and Rac1(GTP) (Figure 4F), consistent with the formation of a membrane-bound PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) ternary complex.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Covalent conjugation of pY peptides to supported lipid bilayers increased the rate of PI(3,4,5)P3 production by 207-fold compared to 10 µM pY in solution.
source: By contrast, covalent conjugation of pY peptides to supported lipid bilayers increased the rate of PI(3,4,5)P3 production by 207-fold (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-2C.

claim: pY alone provided the strongest stimulation of PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity when comparing individual signaling inputs – pY, Rac1(GTP), and GβGγ.
source: Comparing the lipid kinase activity of PI3Kβ measured in the presence of individual signaling inputs – pY, Rac1(GTP), and GβGγ – revealed that pY alone provided the strongest stimulation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GβGγ alone could subtly stimulate PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity without strongly enhancing membrane PI3Kβ localization.
source: Similar to previous observations (Dbouk et al., 2012), we found that GβGγ alone could subtly stimulate PI3Kβ lipid kinase activity, without strongly enhancing membrane PI3Kβ localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and cited previous work.

claim: The PI3Kβ (K532D, K533D) mutant that was unable to interact with GβGγ was insensitive to GβGγ-mediated activation.
source: By contrast, the PI3Kβ (K532D, K533D) mutant that was unable to interact with GβGγ was insensitive to GβGγ-mediated activation (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: After accounting for the 1.8-fold difference in Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane localization comparing pY-Rac1(GDP) and pY-Rac1(GTP) membranes, a 4.3-fold increase in PI3Kβ activity was calculated that was dependent on Rac1(GTP).
source: After accounting for the 1.8-fold difference in Dy647-PI3Kβ membrane localization comparing pY-Rac1(GDP) and pY-Rac1(GTP) membranes, we calculated a 4.3-fold increase in PI3Kβ activity that was dependent on Rac1(GTP).
evidence: This is a calculated result based on data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Comparing the activity of Dy647-PI3Kβ on membranes with pY alone or pY-GβGγ, a 22-fold increase in catalytic efficiency was observed for the PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complex.
source: Comparing the activity of Dy647-PI3Kβ on membranes with pY alone or pY-GβGγ, we observed a 22-fold increase in catalytic efficiency comparing the PI3Kβ-pY and PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complexes (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Maximum synergistic activation occurred when GβGγ was present at a density greater than 2400 molecules/µm2.
source: By varying the density of membrane-anchored GβGγ, we determined that maximum synergistic activation occurred when GβGγ was present at a density greater than 2400 molecules/µm2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The kcat of PI3Kβ-pY-GβGγ complex is 57 PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids/s•PI3Kβ.
source: Based on the membrane-bound density of ~0.2 Dy647-PI3Kβ molecules per µm2, we calculate a kcat of 57 PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids/s•PI3Kβ on pY-GβGγ containing membranes.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on experimental data.

claim: The Dy647-PI3Kβ-pY complex had a kcat of 3 PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids/s•PI3Kβ.
source: By contrast, the Dy647-PI3Kβ-pY complex had a kcat of 3 PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids/s•PI3Kβ.
evidence: This is a calculated value based on experimental data.

claim: This is the first study to reconstitute membrane localization and activation of a class 1A PI3K using multiple signaling inputs that are all membrane-tethered in a physiologically relevant configuration.
source: This is the first study to reconstitute membrane localization and activation of a class 1A PI3K using multiple signaling inputs that are all membrane-tethered in a physiologically relevant configurations.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.

claim: The slow rate of PI(3,4,5)P3 production measured for the membrane-tethered pY-PI3Kβ complex suggests that PI(3,4,5)P3 levels are not likely to rise above the global inhibition imposed by lipid phosphatases until synergistic activation of PI3Kβ by RTKs and GPCRs.
source: The slow rate of PI(3,4,5)P3 production we measured for the membrane-tethered pY-PI3Kβ complex suggests that PI(3,4,5)P3 levels are not likely to rise above the global inhibition imposed by lipid phosphatases until synergistic activation of PI3Kβ by RTKs and GPCRs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Loss of PTEN in some cancers could produce an elevated level of PI(3,4,5)P3 due to PI3Kβ being constitutively membrane localized via ligand-independent trans-autophosphorylation of RTKs.
source: However, loss of PTEN in some cancers (Jia et al., 2008) could produce an elevated level of PI(3,4,5)P3 due to PI3Kβ being constitutively membrane localized via ligand-independent trans-autophosphorylation of RTKs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and cited previous work.

claim: When the cellular plasma membrane contains densities of EGFR greater than 2000 receptors/µm2, trans-autophosphorylation and activation can occur in an EGF-independent manner.
source: When the cellular plasma membrane contains densities of EGFR greater than 2000 receptors/µm2, trans-autophosphorylation, and activation can occur in an EGF-independent manner (Endres et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Endres et al., 2013.

claim: Membrane surface densities above the threshold required for spontaneous trans-autophosphorylation of EGFR have been observed in many cancer cells.
source: Membrane surface densities above the threshold required for spontaneous trans-autophosphorylation of EGFR have been observed in many cancer cells (Haigler et al., 1978).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haigler et al., 1978.

claim: The nSH2 and cSH2 domains of class 1A PI3Ks have a conserved peptide motif, FLVR, that mediates the interaction with tyrosine phosphorylated peptides.
source: The SH2 domains of class 1A PI3Ks have a conserved peptide motif, FLVR, that mediates the interaction with tyrosine phosphorylated peptides (Bradshaw et al., 1999; Waksman et al., 1992; Rameh et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutating the arginine to alanine (FLVA mutant) prevents the interaction with pY peptides for both PI3Kα and PI3Kβ.
source: Mutating the arginine to alanine (FLVA mutant) prevents the interaction with pY peptides for both PI3Kα and PI3Kβ (Yu et al., 1998; Dornan et al., 2020; Nolte et al., 1996; Zhang et al., 2011; Breeze et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The tandem SH2 domains of ZAP-70 can bind to a doubly phosphorylated chain derived from the TCR with only 11 amino acids spacing between the two tyrosine phosphorylation sites.
source: The tandem SH2 domains of ZAP-70 can bind to a doubly phosphorylated chain derived from the TCR with only 11 amino acids spacing between the two tyrosine phosphorylation sites (Hatada et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hatada et al., 1995.

claim: In the PDGFR-derived pY peptide that binds p85α, 10 amino acids separate the two tyrosine phosphorylated residues.
source: In the case of our PDGFR-derived pY peptide that binds p85α, 10 amino acids separate the two tyrosine phosphorylated residues.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental reagent used in the study.

claim: Solution pY did not strongly enhance membrane binding of Dy647-PI3Kβ on GβGγ-containing membranes in the absence of phosphatidylserine (PS) lipids.
source: Based on the bulk membrane recruitment, solution pY did not strongly enhance membrane binding of Dy647-PI3Kβ on GβGγ-containing membranes in the absence of phosphatidylserine (PS) lipids (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When measured on a membrane containing 20% PS, a significant enhancement in Dy647-PI3Kβ localization was observed when solution pY was added to GβGγ-containing membranes.
source: When we measured the interaction between Dy647-PI3Kβ and GβGγ on a membrane containing 20% PS, however, we observed a significant enhancement in Dy647-PI3Kβ localization when solution pY was added (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-1D.

claim: SH2 domain-dependent inhibition of GβGγ binding can be relieved by solution pY, as previously reported.
source: This confirms that SH2 domain-dependent inhibition of GβGγ binding can be relieved by solution pY, as previously reported (Dbouk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and a citation to Dbouk et al., 2012.

claim: A high density of anionic lipids (i.e. PS) was required to facilitate the interaction between pY and GβGγ.
source: However, a high density of anionic lipids (i.e. PS) was required to facilitate the interaction between pY and GβGγ.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The affinity between PI3Kβ and GβGγ is relatively weak, which is consistent with previous structural biochemistry studies.
source: This suggests that the affinity between PI3Kβ and GβGγ is relatively weak, which is consistent with previous structural biochemistry studies (Dbouk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by the current data and a citation to previous work.

claim: Previous hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) experiments could only detect interactions between GβGγ and PI3Kβ (p110β) when the nSH2 domain was either deleted or disengaged from the catalytic domain by a soluble RTK-derived pY peptide.
source: This model is supported by previous hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) experiments that could only detect interactions between GβGγ and PI3Kβ (p110β) when the nSH2 domain was either deleted or disengaged from the catalytic domain by a soluble RTK-derived pY peptide (Dbouk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dbouk et al., 2012.

claim: AlphaFold multimer modeling defined hα1 in the helical domain as the GβGγ binding site on p110β.
source: We examined the putative interface of GβGγ bound to the p110β catalytic domain using AlphaFold multimer (Jumper et al., 2021; Evans et al., 2022; Varadi et al., 2022) which defined hα1 in the helical domain as the binding site.
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold multimer modeling shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The AlphaFold multimer result for the GβGγ binding site was consistent with previous mutagenesis and HDX-MS analysis of GβGγ binding to p110β.
source: This result was consistent with previous mutagenesis and HDX-MS analysis of GβGγ binding to p110β (Dbouk et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dbouk et al., 2012.

claim: The nSH2 domain sterically obstructs the GβGγ binding interface based on comparison of the AlphaFold model to previous X-ray crystallographic data.
source: Comparing our model to previous X-ray crystallographic data of SH2 binding to either p110α and p110β (Zhang et al., 2011; Mandelker et al., 2009) suggested that the nSH2 domain sterically obstructs the GβGγ binding interface (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with GβGγ activation only possible when the nSH2 dissociates from p110β interface.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling and comparison to previous crystallographic data.

claim: The inability of the Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2 domain to bind to pY peptides made the kinase insensitive to synergistic membrane recruitment mediated by pY and GβGγ.
source: Comparing the bulk membrane recruitment of these constructs revealed that the inability of the Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2 domain to bind to pY peptides made the kinase insensitive to synergistic membrane recruitment mediated by pY and GβGγ (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The membrane association dynamics of Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2(R358A) phenocopied a PI3Kβ (K532D, K533D) mutant that lacks the ability to engage GβGγ.
source: Similarly, the membrane association dynamics of Dy647-PI3Kβ nSH2(R358A), phenocopied a PI3Kβ (K532D, K533D) mutant that lacks the ability to engage GβGγ (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: PI3Kβ is the only class IA PI3K shown to interact with Rho-family GTPases, Rac1, and Cdc42.
source: PI3Kβ is the only class IA PI3K shown to interact with Rho-family GTPases, Rac1, and Cdc42 (Fritsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fritsch et al., 2013.

claim: Synergistic activation was dependent on the direct interaction between PI3Kβ and GβGγ.
source: Synergistic activation was dependent on the direct interaction between PI3Kβ and GβGγ (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The enhanced membrane recruitment model has been used to explain the synergistic activation of PI3Kα mediated by pY and Ras(GTP).
source: In the case of PI3Kα, the enhanced membrane recruitment model has been used to explain the synergistic activation mediated by pY and Ras(GTP) (Buckles et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buckles et al., 2017.

claim: The PI3Kα-pY-Ras complex is more robustly localized to membranes compared to the PI3Kα-pY and PI3Kα-Ras complexes, which results in a larger total catalytic output for the system.
source: In other words, the PI3Kα-pY-Ras complex is more robustly localized to membranes compared to the PI3Kα-pY and PI3Kα-Ras complexes, which results in a larger total catalytic output for the system.
evidence: This describes the enhanced membrane recruitment model for PI3Kα.

claim: The Ras binding domain (RBD) of PI3Kα and PI3Kβ are conserved.
source: Although the Ras binding domain (RBD) of PI3Kα and PI3Kβ are conserved, these kinases interact with distinct Ras superfamily GTPases (Fritsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fritsch et al., 2013.

claim: PI3Kα and PI3Kβ interact with distinct Ras superfamily GTPases.
source: Although the Ras binding domain (RBD) of PI3Kα and PI3Kβ are conserved, these kinases interact with distinct Ras superfamily GTPases (Fritsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fritsch et al., 2013.

claim: It's possible that PI3Kα and PI3Kβ display different mechanisms of synergistic activation, which could explain their non-overlapping roles in cell signaling.
source: Therefore, it's possible that PI3Kα and PI3Kβ display different mechanisms of synergistic activation, which could explain their non-overlapping roles in cell signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: Studies of PI3Kβ mouse knock-in mutations in primary macrophages and neutrophils have shown that robust PI3Kβ activation requires coincident activation through the RTK and GPCR signaling pathways.
source: Studies of PI3Kβ mouse knock-in mutations in primary macrophages and neutrophils have shown that robust PI3Kβ activation requires coincident activation through the RTK and GPCR signaling pathways (Houslay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Houslay et al., 2016.

claim: Robust PI3Kβ activation most strongly depends on the ability of PI3Kβ to bind GβGγ and, to a lesser extent, Rac1/Cdc42.
source: This response most strongly depends on the ability of PI3Kβ to bind GβGγ and, to a lesser extent, Rac1/Cdc42 (Houslay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Houslay et al., 2016.

claim: A similar mechanism of synergistic activation has been reported for PI3Kγ in the presence of H-Ras(GTP) and GβGγ.
source: A similar mechanism of synergistic activation has been reported for PI3Kγ in the presence of H-Ras(GTP) and GβGγ (Suire and Lécureuil, 2012; Rathinaswamy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suire and Lécureuil, 2012 and Rathinaswamy et al., 2021.

claim: RTK activation by insulin, PDGF, or EGF show little PI3Kβ dependence for PI(3,4,5)P3 production in cellular measurements.
source: This is consistent with cellular measurements showing that RTK activation by insulin (Knight et al., 2006), PDGF (Guillermet-Guibert et al., 2008), or EGF (Ciraolo et al., 2008) show little PI3Kβ dependence for PI(3,4,5)P3 production.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous cellular studies.

claim: The dominant role of PI3Kα in controlling PI(3,4,5)P3 production downstream of RTKs can mask the contribution from PI3Kβ in some cell types.
source: Although the dominant role of PI3Kα in controlling PI(3,4,5)P3 production downstream of RTKs can mask the contribution from PI3Kβ in some cell types, these results highlight the need for PI3Kβ to be synergistically activated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of previous cellular studies.

claim: After accounting for the ~1.8-fold increase in membrane localization between PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) and PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GDP), a kcat of 13 PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids/sec per PI3Kβ was calculated for the Rac1(GTP)-dependent activation.
source: After accounting for the ~1.8-fold increase in membrane localization between PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GTP) and PI3Kβ-pY-Rac1(GDP), we calculated a 4.3-fold increase in kcat (13 PI(3,4,5)P3 lipids/sec per PI3Kβ) that was dependent on engaging Rac1(GTP).
evidence: This is a calculated value based on experimental data.

claim: PI3Kβ-pY complex association with either Rac1(GTP) or GβGγ allosterically modulates PI3Kβ, making it more catalytically efficient.
source: Together, these results indicate that PI3Kβ-pY complex association with either Rac1(GTP) or GβGγ allosterically modulates PI3Kβ, making it more catalytically efficient.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the kinetic data in Figure 5.

claim: The nSH2 and cSH2 domains of p85α robustly bind pY residues with a methionine in the +3 position (pYXXM).
source: Biochemistry studies indicate that the nSH2 and cSH2 domains of p85α robustly bind pY residues with a methionine in the +3 position (pYXXM) (Breeze et al., 1996; Nolte et al., 1996; Backer et al., 1992; Fantl et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous biochemistry studies.

claim: The p85α subunit is predicted to interact with the broad repertoire of receptors that contain immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) bearing the pYXX(L/I) motif.
source: The p85α subunit is also predicted to interact with the broad repertoire of receptors that contain immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) baring the pYXX(L/I) motif (Reth, 1989; Osman et al., 1996; Zenner et al., 1996; Love and Hayes, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human neutrophils express at least six different Fc receptors (FcRs) that all contain phosphorylated ITAMs that can potentially facilitate membrane localization of class 1A PI3Ks based on RNA seq data.
source: Based on RNA seq data, human neutrophils express at least six different Fc receptors (FcRs) that all contain phosphorylated ITAMs that can potentially facilitate membrane localization of class 1A PI3Ks (Rincón et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rincón et al., 2018.

claim: A variety of human diseases result from the overexpression of RTKs, especially the epithelial growth factor receptor (EGFR).
source: A variety of human diseases result from the overexpression of RTKs, especially the epithelial growth factor receptor (EGFR) (Sauter et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sauter et al., 1996.

claim: In disease states with high EGFR density, PI3K is expected to localize to the plasma membrane in the absence of ligand-induced RTK or GPCR signaling.
source: In these disease states, PI3K is expected to localize to the plasma membrane in the absence of ligand-induced RTK or GPCR signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental findings and knowledge of EGFR biology.
